newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: British bankers try new arenas to beat competition.
newsitem.headline: British bankers try new arenas to beat competition.

text.p: The competition driving the British banking industry has meant bankers are willing to test different waters and face start up losses in order not to get left behind.

British bankers at a financial seminar organised by NCR on Friday made it clear that, while they may have different motivations, they have to be involved in all the new "delivery channels" that are developing.

"One needs to be in all of them, but if you analyse where people buy their financial services, they still buy the bulk of them from traditional banks and building societies," said Peter Birch, chief executive of Abbey National, one of Britain's biggest financial providers.
Abbey has developed a link with supermarket chain Safeway plc to offer services via the store's ABC card which pays customers five percent interest on balances up to 600 pounds.
Birch is unconcerned that the link is marketed using the Safeway name.
"There are two or three big supermarket chains in the UK and we'd rather be there than a competitor bank," he said.

Barclays, another major player in the British financial scene, has said it has no plans for a supermarket link but is considering putting branches into stores in a move comparable to the actions of Wells Fargo bank in the U.S.
The Halifax, Britain's biggest mortgage lender, which on Monday will make its stock market value, has also said it is not interested.

But these banks already have a big presence and the two major Scottish banks, Bank of Scotland and Royal Bank of Scotland, have taken the opportunity to do business in England where they have little representation on the retail side.
BOS has teamed up with J Sainsbury while RBOS is linked to Britain's biggest supermarket chain Tesco.

"We don't know if it will be successful," said George Mathewson chief executive of Royal Bank "We only have 2.5 million retail customers in the bank, they have 12 million in Tesco". Mathewson says the tie-up could provide a large proportion of the banks profits in years to come and obviously hopes this might help plug the weakness of a lack of retail mass south of the border.
"It has to be worth a go -- the downside is only about 25 million pounds and God knows what the upside might be," Mathewson said.

The supermarket bankers are confident they will be able to move on from offering accounts paying top interest rates to selling a variety of financial products, principally via low cost telephone delivery.

Sainsburys Bank, the venture between Sainsbury and BOS, is experimenting with various formats, one of which will include Sainsbury staff trained to provide basic help on financial matters to customers.
But its chief executive Rodger Mcarthur, obviously wants to avoid increasing his current staff of just 24.
Sainsburys Bank is paying 5.75 percent to depositors, compared to a bank base rate of 6.25 percent, and sees no profit until the turn of year three.
"Those are very sharp margins but we are looking to cross-sell off that obviously," Mcarthur told Reuters.
He anticipates a start up loss of between 15 and 20 million pounds in the first year but says this is acceptable in terms of acquisition cost per account.
Sainsburys will launch personal loans at competitive rates in June, mortgages in July and insurance by the end of the summer though Mcarthur would not be drawn on who the insurance partner would be.
"Its early days, we are all feeling our way," said Abbey's Birch "but we do have a toe in the water".
